title: Does the block producer correctly reject blocks with malformed deposit data rather than propagating invalid blocks?

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Abstract interpretation analysis reveals critical state-space anomalies in deposit validation during block production and P2P validation. The system exhibits WEAK VALIDATION in the block producer path where malformed deposit data can bypass local validation and be included in proposed blocks. While P2P validation has stronger checks, the asymmetry creates a vulnerability window where malicious block producers can construct blocks with invalid deposits that pass initial checks but fail during state transition.

transformations: 1. Filter by index range (beaconState.Eth1DepositIndex() to canonicalEth1Data.DepositCount)
3. Return deposits WITHOUT signature or data field validation
variable_analysis.anomaly_details: The deposits() function in block production does NOT validate deposit signatures or check for malformed deposit data fields (PublicKey, WithdrawalCredentials, Amount, Signature). It only validates Merkle proof construction and index ordering. This creates an abstract state where deposits ∈ {VALID_PROOF ∩ (VALID_SIG ∪ INVALID_SIG ∪ MALFORMED)} instead of the expected {VALID_PROOF ∩ VALID_SIG}.

state_space_analysis.actual_state: ∀ deposit ∈ block.deposits: ValidMerkleProof(deposit) [signatures and data fields unchecked in producer]
state_space_analysis.violation: Block producer can create blocks where ValidMerkleProof(deposit) = true BUT ValidSignature(deposit) = false OR WellFormed(deposit.Data) = false
reachable_bad_states: Block with nil deposit.Data (line 44-46 check only happens in ProcessDeposits, not in producer)
Block with invalid BLS public key format (uncaught until bls.PublicKeyFromBytes() in verifyDepositDataWithDomain)
Block with malformed signature bytes (uncaught until signature verification)
Block with invalid withdrawal credentials format

validation_layers.deposit_checks: NONE - deposits not validated at P2P layer

checks: Nil deposit data check (line 44-46 in electra/deposits.go)
validation_layers.deposit_checks: FULL - but only during state transition, not P2P gossip

variable_analysis.anomaly_details: P2P validation (validateBeaconBlock) does NOT validate deposits, only block-level fields. Deposit validation only occurs during state transition (ProcessDeposits). This creates a temporal gap where invalid blocks can propagate through P2P gossip before being rejected during state application.

state_space_analysis.expected_invariant: Block rejected at P2P layer if ANY operation (including deposits) is invalid
state_space_analysis.actual_state: Block accepted at P2P layer if block-level validation passes, regardless of deposit validity
state_space_analysis.violation: Malformed deposit blocks can propagate through gossip network before being rejected during state transition
state_space_analysis.attack_vector: Malicious proposer constructs block with deposits where: ValidMerkleProof = true, ValidBlockSig = true, ValidDeposit = false. Block passes P2P validation (lines 254-313) but fails state transition, wasting network resources.

control_flow: 2. If batch verification fails, set allSignaturesVerified = false
3. Fall back to individual verification per deposit (line 47)
4. Individual ProcessDeposit can SILENTLY SKIP invalid deposits (line 140 in electra/deposits.go)
variable_analysis.anomaly_details: Batch signature verification failure (line 38-41) returns (false, nil) rather than rejecting the block. The system then processes deposits individually where IsValidDepositSignature returning false causes the deposit to be SKIPPED (line 140: 'return beaconState, nil') rather than the block being REJECTED. This means a block with ONE malformed deposit can still be processed with that deposit ignored.

state_space_analysis.expected_invariant: Block with ANY invalid deposit is REJECTED
state_space_analysis.actual_state: Block with invalid deposits is ACCEPTED with invalid deposits SKIPPED
state_space_analysis.violation: State transition succeeds even when deposits fail signature verification, just skipping them. This diverges from expected behavior where malformed data should cause block rejection.
reachable_states: State1: All deposits valid → All deposits processed
State2: Some deposits invalid → Valid deposits processed, invalid skipped (state accepted)
State3: All deposits invalid → No deposits processed (state accepted, empty result)
state_space_analysis.correctness_issue: Spec expects deposit validation to be MANDATORY. Silently skipping deposits may cause state divergence across clients if not all implement the same 'skip on invalid' logic.

variable_analysis.safety_check: if d == nil || d.Data == nil { return errors.New('got a nil deposit in block') }
control_flow_order: 1. Block producer constructs deposits via deposits() function (proposer_deposits.go:78-172)
2. Deposits added to block WITHOUT nil checking
3. Block propagated via P2P (validate_beacon_blocks.go) WITHOUT deposit validation
5. Nil check FIRST occurs at line 44-46
variable_analysis.anomaly_details: Nil deposit or nil deposit.Data can be included in a block by producer, propagate through P2P validation, and only get caught during state transition. This wastes network bandwidth and processing time. The abstract state allows Deposit ∈ {nil} ∪ {Data: nil} to enter the system until the state transition boundary.

state_space_analysis.expected_invariant: ∀ deposit ∈ block.deposits: deposit ≠ nil ∧ deposit.Data ≠ nil (enforced at block creation)
state_space_analysis.actual_state: Nil deposits can exist in block body and only caught at state transition
state_space_analysis.violation: Block creation and P2P validation do not enforce deposit ≠ nil invariant
state_space_analysis.attack_vector: Malicious block producer crafts deposits array with nil entries or entries with nil Data. Block passes P2P checks but fails state transition after propagating through network.

validation_sequence: 4. Verify merkle proof against deposit root (line 115-121)
variable_analysis.anomaly_details: Merkle proof is verified BEFORE signature verification in the deposit processing pipeline. If signature check is deferred or skipped (as in the batch verification fallback case), a deposit with valid merkle proof but invalid signature can partially progress through the system. The abstract state allows: {ValidMerkleProof ∧ InvalidSignature} as an intermediate reachable state.

state_space_analysis.expected_invariant: Signature validation should gate all further processing
state_space_analysis.actual_state: Merkle validation occurs first, signature validation can be deferred/skipped
state_space_analysis.violation: Resource expenditure (merkle tree operations) occurs before cryptographic validation
state_space_analysis.dos_vector: Attacker can construct deposits with valid merkle proofs but invalid signatures, forcing nodes to perform expensive merkle verifications before rejecting based on signature

processing: 2. Parse as BLS PublicKey via bls.PublicKeyFromBytes (line 149-152)
3. If parsing FAILS, return error immediately
output_states: Success: All keys parsed → pks[] contains valid keys → batch verify signatures
Failure: Any key malformed → bls.PublicKeyFromBytes returns error → entire batch fails (line 151)

variable_analysis.anomaly_details: If even ONE deposit has a malformed public key, the entire batch verification fails at line 151. This causes the system to downgrade from batch verification (O(n) BLS aggregation) to individual verification (O(n) BLS verifications). An attacker can force this expensive downgrade by including a single malformed key among valid deposits.

state_space_analysis.expected_behavior: Batch verification should handle mixed valid/invalid deposits gracefully
state_space_analysis.actual_behavior: Single malformed deposit forces fallback to individual verification for ALL deposits in the block
state_space_analysis.violation: Performance degradation attack: one bad deposit → O(n) cost increase for block processing
state_space_analysis.attack_scenario: Malicious proposer includes 1 deposit with malformed pubkey + N-1 valid deposits → Forces all nodes to do individual signature verification instead of batch, increasing CPU cost by ~10-100x depending on BLS implementation

block_production_path.validation_strength: WEAK - Only merkle proof construction, no signature or data validation

p2p_validation_path.validation_strength: NONE for deposits - Block-level checks only

identified_vulnerabilities.title: Block Producer Does Not Validate Deposit Signatures
identified_vulnerabilities.description: The block producer's deposits() function (proposer_deposits.go:78-172) does not validate deposit signatures or check for malformed deposit data. It only ensures merkle proofs can be constructed. This allows a block producer to include deposits with invalid signatures or malformed data fields.
identified_vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Malicious block producer fetches pending deposits, constructs valid merkle proofs, but includes deposits with corrupted signatures or nil data fields. The block is created successfully and propagated via P2P.
identified_vulnerabilities.impact: Network bandwidth waste, honest node processing overhead, potential state divergence if clients handle invalid deposits differently

identified_vulnerabilities.title: P2P Validation Does Not Check Deposits
identified_vulnerabilities.description: The P2P block validation (validateBeaconBlock in validate_beacon_blocks.go) does not perform ANY deposit-specific validation. Blocks with malformed deposits pass P2P validation and propagate through the network before being rejected during state transition.
identified_vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Malicious proposer creates block with deposits that have: (1) nil Data pointers, (2) malformed BLS public keys, (3) invalid signatures but valid merkle proofs. Block passes P2P validation (lines 254-313) and propagates to all peers before each peer rejects it during state transition.
identified_vulnerabilities.impact: Network-wide DoS: All nodes waste bandwidth receiving and forwarding invalid blocks, CPU time on initial validation, and storage for temporary pending blocks

identified_vulnerabilities.title: Malformed Deposits Cause Batch Verification Downgrade
identified_vulnerabilities.description: A single deposit with a malformed public key causes bls.PublicKeyFromBytes() to fail (deposit.go:151), which causes the entire batch signature verification to fail and downgrade to expensive individual verification for ALL deposits in the block.
identified_vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Attacker includes 1 deposit with malformed pubkey + 15 valid deposits. This forces all nodes to perform 16 individual BLS signature verifications instead of 1 batch verification, increasing CPU cost by ~10-100x.
identified_vulnerabilities.impact: CPU exhaustion DoS, block processing delays, potential for chain stall if enough malicious blocks are produced

identified_vulnerabilities.title: Invalid Deposits Silently Skipped Instead of Block Rejection
identified_vulnerabilities.description: When a deposit fails signature validation during state transition, it is SKIPPED (electra/deposits.go:140) rather than causing block rejection. This means blocks with invalid deposits are accepted into the chain with those deposits ignored.
identified_vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Block producer includes deposits with invalid signatures. Block is processed successfully but deposits are silently dropped. This violates the expectation that all deposits in a valid block are valid deposits.
identified_vulnerabilities.impact: Potential state divergence if clients disagree on skip behavior, user deposits lost if depositor is unaware their deposit was skipped, violation of deposit processing guarantees

identified_vulnerabilities.title: Nil Deposit Data Can Propagate Through P2P
identified_vulnerabilities.description: Deposits with nil pointers (deposit == nil or deposit.Data == nil) can be included in blocks, pass P2P validation, and only get caught at state transition (electra/deposits.go:44-46). This wastes network resources.
identified_vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Malicious proposer crafts a block with deposits array containing nil entries or entries with nil Data. Block propagates through P2P network, all peers download and forward it, then all peers reject it during state transition.
identified_vulnerabilities.impact: Network-wide bandwidth waste, P2P amplification attack (one malicious block → N peer downloads)

recommendations.recommendation: Add deposit validation to block production path
recommendations.details: Before returning deposits in the deposits() function, validate: (1) deposit != nil && deposit.Data != nil, (2) BLS public key is well-formed via bls.PublicKeyFromBytes(), (3) All data fields are non-nil and within expected ranges. This prevents malformed deposits from being included in produced blocks.
recommendations.code_change: Add validation loop after line 169: for each deposit, verify deposit.Data != nil, validate BLS pubkey format, check signature if computational budget allows (or at minimum check key format).

recommendations.recommendation: Add deposit validation to P2P block validation
recommendations.details: Add a deposit validation step in validateBeaconBlock that checks: (1) No nil deposits or deposit.Data, (2) BLS public keys are well-formed, (3) Deposit merkle proofs are valid against eth1_data.deposit_root. This prevents malformed blocks from propagating through gossip.
recommendations.code_change: After line 258 (validateDenebBeaconBlock), add validateBlockDeposits(blk) that performs basic deposit sanity checks. This prevents P2P propagation of blocks with obviously malformed deposits.

recommendations.recommendation: Fail-fast on malformed deposits instead of skipping
recommendations.details: Change behavior from 'skip invalid deposit' to 'reject block with invalid deposit'. When IsValidDepositSignature returns false (line 139), return an error instead of returning (beaconState, nil). This ensures blocks with invalid deposits are rejected rather than accepted with deposits skipped.
recommendations.code_change: At line 140, change 'return beaconState, nil' to 'return nil, errors.New("deposit signature verification failed")'. This causes block rejection instead of silent skipping.

recommendations.details: Instead of failing entire batch when one pubkey is malformed, identify and isolate the malformed deposit, verify the rest in batch, and explicitly reject the block due to the malformed deposit. This prevents DoS via batch verification downgrade while still rejecting invalid blocks.
recommendations.code_change: Wrap bls.PublicKeyFromBytes() in a try-catch equivalent, collect malformed deposit indices, batch-verify valid deposits, then return error indicating which deposits were malformed. This maintains batch verification performance while providing better error reporting.

recommendations.recommendation: Add nil checks at block construction
recommendations.details: After deposits are retrieved and merkle proofs constructed (line 211), add a validation loop to ensure no nil deposits or deposit.Data before setting them on the block. This prevents nil deposits from ever entering a block.
recommendations.code_change: After line 211 (packDepositsAndAttestations), add: for i, d := range deposits { if d == nil || d.Data == nil { return nil, errors.Errorf("nil deposit at index %d", i) } }. This catches nil deposits at construction time.

abstract_interpretation_notes.analysis_approach: Analyzed deposit data flow through three critical paths: (1) block production, (2) P2P validation, (3) state transition. Tracked abstract domains for deposit objects, validation states, and error handling modes.
key_insights: Validation asymmetry: Strong validation during state transition, weak/absent validation during production and P2P propagation
Temporal vulnerability window: Malformed deposits can exist in-flight in the P2P network before being rejected
Silent failure mode: Invalid deposits are skipped rather than causing block rejection, violating principle of explicit failure
Performance attack surface: Batch verification downgrade can be triggered by single malformed deposit among many valid ones
Defense-in-depth failure: Lack of validation at block production and P2P layers means state transition is single point of defense
abstract_interpretation_notes.state_space_complexity: The combination of three validation paths with different strength creates a large state space of reachable configurations. A block can be in states: {PRODUCED, P2P_VALIDATED, STATE_ACCEPTED, STATE_REJECTED} with deposits in states: {WELL_FORMED, MALFORMED_KEYS, MALFORMED_DATA, NIL, INVALID_SIG}. The cross-product creates ~20 reachable state combinations, many of which are security-relevant.
